channel.title: ResearchBuzz - Transformed
channel.description: News and resources covering social media, search engines, databases, archives, and other such information collections. Since 1998.

item.title: Child advocacy group launches ‘living resource’ for childhood well-being data
item.description: Alabama Reflector: “Alabama’s leading source of children’s well-being data and research plans to launch a new online data center to increase access to up-to-date information, the group announced Wednesday. VOICES for Alabama’s Children, a nonprofit organization, is moving its annual research project to an online dashboard that can be updated as new data becomes available, becoming a ‘living resource.'”

item.title: Buddy Icon Archive
item.description: Found in my Calishat Snaps: From the site’s short history of AIM buddy icons: “The canvas was so small that every decision became emphatic. Surviving client documentation describes images between 48×48 and 50×50 pixels. A face needed a close crop; text needed blunt contrast; an idea often had to survive in a single glance. Animated GIFs turned that square into a tiny cinematic form. A 2003 essay about BadassBuddy noticed camera movement, cuts, lighting, and short narratives squeezed into the icon window. Some loops lasted only a few seconds. That was enough time for a reaction, a punch line, a declaration of love, or a cartoon character to suffer a compact but complete misfortune.”

item.title: Meta Doesn’t Want to Be a Social Media Company Anymore
item.description: Mother Jones: “Like virtually every other tech company, then, Meta executives have turned from social media as their core product, to a gauzy, pie-eyed future of AI as the future of work, business and everything else. Laws, legislation and jury settlements are often backwards-looking when it comes to tech companies. This particular settlement attempts to mitigate the harm of their current products, while companies like Meta are already focused, for better or much more likely worse, on what’s next.”

item.title: ‘Thin Air,’ Real Money: Donald Trump’s Crypto Products Have Left Investors at Least $4.7 Billion Underwater
item.description: Public Citizen: “According to Public Citizen’s analysis, Trump’s crypto schemes have left investors at least an estimated $4.7 billion underwater. These losses are largely unrealized and, in the case of his meme coin, reflect wealth transferred to a small group of early buyers rather than money that simply vanished.”

item.title: To Silicon Valley, anything could be a ‘psyop’
item.description: CNN: “Most Americans don’t want AI data centers near them. There are plenty of well-reported reasons why: People may be concerned about the environmental impacts, or angry over AI companies threatening mass unemployment and skeptical of promises that data centers will usher in a jobs boom. They could be worried about higher utility bills. Then there’s the noise. The constant, maddening noise. But in Silicon Valley, a different, more sinister explanation for the anti-data center movement has taken hold.”

item.title: Flipboard acquires Graze, the feed builder working to monetize the open social web
item.description: TechCrunch: “Flipboard, the news magazine software company that has more recently invested in the open social web — the umbrella term for social platforms that let users, not one company, control their own data and audience — is making another big bet on that ecosystem. The company on Wednesday announced it’s acquiring the Portland-based feed-building startup Graze, which has been working to monetize the open social web by allowing feed creators to support themselves via ads.”

item.title: Three UK airports hit by cyber-attack with data of 8.7m customers accessed
item.description: The Guardian: “Manchester, London Stansted and East Midlands airports have been hit by a cyber-attack in which hackers accessed the data of about 8.7 million customers.”

item.title: Speed Art Museum begins repatriation of 24 Native American cultural items
item.description: Spectrum News: “The Speed Art Museum is returning 24 cultural items to the Southern Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes as part of a federal repatriation process under the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act.”

item.title: Creating an Open-source Blogging Studies Syllabus
item.description: Brennan.Day: “The premise for this is rather simple: I am going to create a static site that will act as the syllabus and curriculum for Blogging Studies, and it will include lessons/lectures, assignments, recommended readings, and methods for class participation. Blogging Studies is a term I coined myself, and I define it as the study and practice of writing craft and independent online publishing as a single, integrated discipline, treating the blog post medium as a legitimate unit of scholarly and creative work.”

item.title: An otter, a beaver — and now a mink spotted in the Bronx
item.description: Gothamist: “A week after announcing his camera trap had captured the first otter in the Bronx River in a century, a local wildlife researcher was surprised to see a new face in his lens: an American mink.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Data For Dummies: Hawaiʻi Facts For Those Of Us Who Can’t Read Spreadsheets
item.description: Honolulu Civil Beat: “Now that another primary election has come and gone, I’ve been wondering: Is Hawaiʻi still the worst in the nation when it comes to voter turnout? Fortunately, the folks who built Hawaiʻi Dashboard, a cool new database of key Hawaiʻi facts, figures and trends, were reading my mind.”

item.title: Ministry for Foreign Affairs makes Raoul Wallenberg documents available in new database
item.description: Government Offices of Sweden: “On Raoul Wallenberg Day, 27 August, the Ministry for Foreign Affairs is presenting a new digital database containing the documents in the Raoul Wallenberg case preserved in the Ministry’s archives. The collection comprises documents from the period 1945–2018, approximately 71 000 pages in several languages, and provides researchers, journalists and the public with online access to material that sheds light on both Mr Wallenberg’s efforts during the Second World War and the long-standing efforts to clarify his fate.”

item.title: [Exclusive] Google builds Korea team for full-functioning Maps service
item.description: Korea Herald: “Google is stepping up preparations to expand Google Maps in South Korea by recruiting a senior partnerships manager, as the company says it is ‘officially launching full-functioning Google Maps capabilities’ in the country.”

item.title: Judge dismisses lawsuit by Elon Musk’s X challenging New York hate speech law
item.description: Reuters: “A U.S. judge on Wednesday dismissed a lawsuit by Elon Musk’s ​X seeking to void a New York state law requiring social media ‌companies to disclose how they monitor hate speech, extremism, harassment, foreign political interference and disinformation.”

item.title: White House teleprompter operator ordered to pay $172K for placing prediction market bets on Trump’s speeches
item.description: NBC News: “A teleprompter operator for President Donald Trump who made online prediction trades based on information from upcoming speeches has been ordered to pay $172,000, a federal agency said Friday night. Gabriel Perez used ‘material, nonpublic information’ he obtained through his job to place ‘trades’ on a prediction market, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission said in a news release.”

item.title: Google Search Showing Fewer PDF Files. But Why?
item.description: Search Engine Roundtable: “Google seems to be showing fewer and fewer PDF files, and when it does show PDF files, it seems not to show them from some pretty important sites, like IRS.gov, New York State, and some others. But in some cases we are seeing Google show PDF documents, without you having to explicitly filter for PDF file types.”

item.title: What’s hot on TikTok LIVE? You can find out through a new newsletter.
item.description: Tubefilter: “TikTok has a plan to make live streaming less intimidating for new users, and that plan involves Substack. The media platform is the home of The Creator’s Cut, a newsletter that shares tips and best practices related to TikTok LIVE.”

item.title: Gov. Abbott blocks state agencies from spending money on Flock cameras
item.description: Texas Tribune: “Gov. Greg Abbott has ordered all state agencies to pause funding for Flock cameras as scrutiny over the AI-powered surveillance devices has mounted. The order came as The Texas Tribune was preparing to publish an investigation detailing how a state agency has devoted at least $30 million to building up the state’s Flock surveillance network by providing grants to local police departments.”

item.title: Prediction Markets Should Be Regulated as Gambling, Appeals Court Says
item.description: New York Times: This link goes to a gift article. “A federal appeals court ruled on Friday that states had the ability to regulate prediction markets, a win for the states in an ongoing battle with federal regulators over who had authority over popular wagering platforms. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit in San Francisco rejected Kalshi’s request for relief against Nevada’s gambling laws, after the state sued the company in February for ‘unlicensed operations.'”

item.title: Info for confidential voters was made public in Colorado secretary of state web update, office confirms
item.description: Denver Post: “The Colorado Secretary of State’s Office made information for more than 130,000 confidential voters publicly accessible for over a week because of an error in updating a voter registration tool, agency officials said Thursday. Agency staff confirmed that 59 voter profiles for people who had requested that their records not be publicly disclosed were accessed between Aug. 14 and late Tuesday afternoon, when the problem was discovered.”

item.title: Belize Establishes First National Music Archive
item.description: San Pedro Sun: “Belize officially marked a major step in preserving its cultural heritage on August 24th, when Honorable Francis Fonseca, Minister of Culture, announced the establishment of the country’s first Belize Music Archive and the National Recording Treasures of Belize. The initiative was launched through the Belize Music Project, with a new archive laboratory opened at the Belize Archives and Records Service in Belmopan.”

item.title: Mapping the Survivors: Rene Ligon’s Quest to Document the World’s Remaining Douglas DC-3s
item.description: Vintage Aviation News: “What began as a search for airworthy Douglas DC-3s to photograph has grown into a worldwide research project. Aviation photographer Rene Ligon has documented nearly 600 surviving airframes—from working transports and museum exhibits to forgotten wrecks in remote locations.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: The 14,000 followers of ‘Historic Boston Archives’ are calling out its insane AI videos
item.description: Boston.com: “Whoever runs the Facebook page ‘Historical Boston Archives’ probably didn’t think they were fooling anybody when they posted old photos of Boston brought to life on video — they probably just thought they looked cool. But that hasn’t stopped many of its 14,000 followers from calling the posts out as ‘AI slop,’ some of them in hilarious fashion.”

item.title: Photos of ‘Cat in the Hat Serial Killer’ Are AI-Generated, Police Say
item.description: PetaPixel: “AI-generated pictures and videos purporting to show one of Dr. Seuss’ characters as a serial killer have prompted police in the U.K. and Ireland to state that ‘Cat in the Hat was not in your driveway.'”

item.title: More Arkansas communities putting data centers on hold
item.description: Arkansas Times: “The number of Arkansas communities rejecting or imposing new limits on data centers is growing faster than the list of places considering such projects publicly. Madison County joined four other counties in passing a three-year moratorium on data center projects last week, though it doesn’t have any known projects in development. The pause is the second-longest in the state; only Independence County’s is longer.”

item.title: One of East Coast’s largest data centers accused of ‘violating federal law’
item.description: Floodlight: “The largest planned AI data center in New Jersey is being accused of violating federal law after a Floodlight visual investigation found the site running dozens of unpermitted gas-powered generators. Thermal drone footage we captured last week showed the partly completed DataOne facility in Vineland was operating at least 45 of the site’s 62 generators at the time.”

item.title: Blue-collar jobs are the new flashpoint in data-center fight
item.description: Wall Street Journal: “Nationwide resistance to the construction has grown so broad that politicians on both sides of the aisle have halted approvals or tightened oversight as midterm elections approach. Unions and construction trade groups are now entering the fray from the other side, warning that such actions endanger thousands of building-related jobs. They are threatening to withhold support of candidates opposing the data-center projects.”

item.title: Data center developers are pushing Pa. government officials to sign secrecy agreements. At least some are saying yes.
item.description: River Reporter: “Public records requests filed by Spotlight PA found at least eight NDAs signed by township, county, and Shapiro administration officials for data center projects. Why they signed and whether the NDA shaped an eventual deal isn’t always clear. Only two lawmakers who signed such agreements responded to the newsroom’s requests for comment.”

item.title: New state law to protect consumers from data center costs faces its first test
item.description: Florida Trib: “The case before Florida’s Public Service Commission is weighing whether Duke Energy plans to do enough to shield customers from the costs of data centers – probing how state regulators will enforce a law intended to ensure that the energy-intensive facilities and not regular ratepayers are the ones covering the data center costs.”

item.title: Colorado Sen. Cathy Kipp submits first complaint under state’s deepfake disclosure law
item.description: Colorado Newsline: “Sen. Cathy Kipp, a Fort Collins Democrat, filed a complaint with the office on Aug. 5 against the Independence Institute, as first reported by CBS Colorado. She alleges that a video posted to multiple Independence Institute social media accounts violates a 2024 law that requires disclosure on deepfake videos of candidates within 90 days of a general election.”

item.title: ‘It’s high-tech theft’: As AI music booms, Canadian artists demand consent, transparency and pay
item.description: Canadian Press: “Cadence Weapon never gave artificial intelligence permission to learn from his music. But the Edmonton-raised rapper, born Rollie Pemberton, says he recently found 129 of his songs in datasets used to train AI music generators. He was alarmed, but not surprised. To Pemberton, it’s part of a broader fight musicians face as AI-generated music floods streaming platforms and companies train models on existing creative work, often without artists’ knowledge or consent.”

item.title: Museums and AI: Critical Decisions
item.description: American Alliance of Museums: “Welcome to CFM’s summer series on all things Artificial Intelligence. To catch up with our coverage so far, read three scenarios of potential AI futures—bright, dark, and muddling through—commentary by Nik Honeysett on how AI is changing how people encounter information; and a tour of the National Archives Museum’s new AI-powered exhibition. Today I’m sharing my working outline of key decisions museums face about the use of artificial intelligence.”

item.title: Your WordPress.com Site Now Works from Inside ChatGPT
item.description: WordPress: No thanks, I’m good. “You can now manage your WordPress.com site from ChatGPT using the new WordPress.com ChatGPT plugin. Set it up once, then talk to your site to publish posts, moderate comments, check traffic, update media, and handle the small jobs that start after the writing ends.”

item.title: Microsoft AI watermarks in Paint and Photos are linked to user IDs, researcher finds
item.description: The Register: “When Anthropic disclosed earlier this month that it would be applying a statistical word-choice watermark to its Claude text output, the company noted that at least 190 AI providers have agreed to abide by Europe’s AI transparency rules. One such company is Microsoft, which has been applying its own form of watermarking to images created with the assistance of AI in its Paint and Photos applications for Windows.”

item.title: OpenAI Has to Answer to Alabama on Hugging Face Hack
item.description: Gizmodo: “OpenAI’s general attitude towards the fact that one of its AI models went rogue and hacked into the systems of the open-source AI platform Hugging Face has been, ‘That’s our bad, but you gotta admit, it’s pretty cool, right?’ The Attorney General of Alabama’s answer to that is a pretty resounding ‘No.’ On Monday, Alabama AG Steve Marshall announced that he had launched an investigation into the incident and is demanding that OpenAI respond.”

item.title: Study: AI growth requires huge electric grid upgrades
item.description: Columbia Missourian: “A new federal report shows the electric grid across much of the country is strained, requiring thousands of miles of new power lines and billions of dollars in investments. The National Transmission Needs Study shows that approximately 4,000 miles of power lines will need to be replaced each year for the next few decades.”

item.title: SLAC researchers develop AI-based tool to compress data without losing detail
item.description: SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory: “Next-generation science experiments will collect more data than ever – so much so that they’ll surpass the capabilities of current data storage and analysis methods. To help, researchers at the Department of Energy’s SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory developed a method to use artificial intelligence to compress large amounts of raw data without losing subtle details critical to scientific discovery.” Good evening, Internet…

item.title: Ohio launches dashboards tracking education, careers of high school grads
item.description: Spectrum News: “Two new resources are now available for Ohioans to gain an insight into student’s education and workforce outcomes after high school. The Ohio Department of Education and Workforce (DEW) Director Stephen D. Dackin announced the launch of Ohio High School Outcomes and Ohio Career and Technical Education Outcomes.”

item.title: Meta is closing a loophole that allowed people to record with their smart glasses’ light covered
item.description: Engadget: “Meta is making yet another change to its smart glasses to try to prevent people from covertly recording others. The company is rolling out a software update that closes one loophole that allowed people to bypass the LED by covering it up while a recording was in progress, according to Alex Himel, Meta’s VP of AR.”

item.title: Extract and Review Web Page Links Using a Bookmarklet
item.description: Adam’s Desk: “I set out to figure out a solution to extract and then review all web page links using a bookmarklet. I’ve found the bookmarklet I created ‘List Page Links’ to be quite useful and figured I should share it with you dear reader. Come along to discover what are bookmarklets, the advantages of this simple bookmarklet, how to install and run it.”

item.title: Dan Rodricks: Launching from Baltimore, an app connecting musicians by the score
item.description: Baltimore Fishbowl: “Imagine that you’re a musician — cellist, pianist, lead guitar in a rock band, Gospel singer, sax player in a jazz ensemble — and you’re practicing some new piece, or even an old one you never quite mastered. Imagine further that you’re stuck somewhere in the sheet music, that you’re playing adagio when you should be at allegro. Imagine being able to instantly find someone somewhere — anywhere in the world — who’s practicing the same piece at the same time you are.”

item.title: Inside the rise of Maine’s partisan ‘pink slime’ news pages
item.description: Sun-Journal: “The Portland Press Herald identified three recently created sites in Maine with the hallmarks of pink slime on both sides of the partisan aisle: Maine Newsroom, the Portland Post and Maine Policy Updates. The sites differ in partisan orientation, source of funding, and the extent to which any editors or authors can be identified. Each page presents itself as a reputable local news source while posting steady streams of politicized news. They are all run by either super PACs, nationwide dark money groups or partisan operatives, all obscuring their roles in swaying Maine’s media ecosystem for political benefit.”

item.title: IRS Website Drops Heavily In Google Search
item.description: Search Engine Roundtable: “Over the past few days, the IRS website (and other government sites) has tanked within Google’s search results. My gut feeling is that the federal government implemented some bot-blocking that was too aggressive and blocked Google, among others, resulting in Google not fully showing the IRS website. I believe the IRS implemented some fixes, and the website is slowly coming back in Google Search.”

item.title: The German Bundestag has copyright problems
item.description: Heise Online: “Suddenly, a part of the Bundestag’s history is missing: Since April, the online archive for the years 2005 to 2016 is no longer available on the Bundestag website. Content ranging from consultation processes to parliamentary biographies has disappeared: the so-called web archive, with which the content of the respective legislative periods of the parliament was frozen in a kind of space-time continuum at the end of each period and preserved for posterity.”

item.title: Fifth Circuit sides with news aggregator in copyright battle
item.description: Courthouse News Service: “News aggregator NewsBreak prevailed Thursday in a copyright dispute with a publisher who took issue with embedded news articles displayed on NewBreak’s app. Emmerich Newspapers, which publishes local newspapers across Mississippi, Louisiana and Arkansas, had challenged a lower court’s decision that NewsBreak did not violate its copyright.”

item.title: Psychologists Examine Downside of Social Media Algorithms
item.description: University of Texas at Dallas: “While social media algorithms have become excellent at matching a user’s viewing habits with targeted, personalized content, psychologists at The University of Texas at Dallas have determined that these algorithms may have a negative influence on a user’s mental health.”

item.title: How Scholars and Musicians Recreated a Song Lost for More Than 400 Years
item.description: Yale University: “From May 14-16, the group worked to contextualize and recreate the Chorus Brasilicus, a song in Tupi—an Indigenous language of Brazil—that was performed before the king of Portugal and Spain in 1619. The lyrics of this song survived in a text describing the play in which it was performed, but the music did not. The effort culminated in a live performance of the reconstructed work and continued in a workshop at the University of Brasília on May 18.” The music is included with the article. It’s a good listen. Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: New digital archive highlights work of Italian artist Augusto Salvatore Oppo
item.description: Artdaily: “A new open digital archive is bringing renewed attention to Augusto Salvatore Oppo (Sassari, 1939–2015), an Italian painter, designer and educator whose work developed over more than five decades but remained largely outside the national art-historical narrative.”

item.title: The Rebrand Registry tracks Microsoft’s endless brand gyrations
item.description: Boing Boing: “Google regularly murders fine products and leaves them for others to bury. Microsoft, though, just renames theirs constantly. The Rebrand Registry now exists to help us keep track of Redmond’s insatiable taste for fresh paint.”

item.title: Google Search Has A Special Dolly Parton Easter Egg
item.description: Search Engine Roundtable: “To commemorate the life of Dolly Parton, Google has released a new easter egg in its search results. If you search for [Dolly Parton] within Google Search, you will see butterflies come up from the bottom of the screen up through the search results page.”

item.title: Legacy Family Tree Webinars introduces Learning Paths
item.description: Genealogy’s Star: “With a library now exceeding 2,700 genealogy webinars, finding a specific entry point or structured educational sequence on Legacy Family Tree Webinars has presented a logistical challenge for many researchers. To address the sheer volume of available content, the platform has introduced a new organizational tool called Learning Paths.”

item.title: How I turned my ancient Windows PC into a Chromebook for free – with FydeOS
item.description: ZDNet: “FydeOS is a Linux-based OS that looks and feels just like ChromeOS, down to the Material Me design. It includes background updates (so you don’t have to worry about remembering to update), seamlessly supports web, Android, and Linux apps, boots in 8 seconds, uses read-only access and ‘virus armour’ for hardened security, FydeOS AI that seamlessly integrates with the OS, and it’s free.”

item.title: Vital Communities enters talks to save town listservs from shutdown
item.description: Valley News: “Talks have started between Vital Communities and a group of Upper Valley residents about preserving the town-specific listservs before the nonprofit pulls the plug…. The organization’s announcement came after it announced last week that it would no longer support the 38 town-specific listservs — where people share town news, business deals and information about lost pets, among other topics — that it has overseen since 2014. Originally, the listservs where scheduled to end last Friday, but after community feedback Vital Communities delayed their demise.”

item.title: Chicago History Museum workers ratify first union contract
item.description: Chicago Sun-Times: “Workers at the Chicago History Museum have ratified their first union contract, after what the union representing the workers called ‘some of the worst anti-union retaliation we’ve seen.’ In May, the National Labor Relations Board issued a rare formal complaint, alleging that under the museum’s previous president, Donald Lassere, management retaliated against employees who voted to unionize in 2025.”

item.title: Governments May Now Take ‘Months or Years’ to Fill Public Records Requests
item.description: Voice of San Diego: “At issue in the case: The California Constitution requires agencies to produce public records ‘promptly.’ But what does that mean? The appeals court’s written ruling said that no timer could be placed on the definition of promptness; it rejected Voice’s argument that it should mean ‘days and weeks’ as opposed to ‘months and years.’ What is prompt, the court found, depends on the nature of the request and “the circumstances of each case.'”

item.title: Twitch and Amazon facing class-action lawsuit over scraping streamers’ content without their consent
item.description: Tubefilter: “A Connecticut-based Twitch streamer has filed a class-action lawsuit against the platform over its recent announcement that creators’ content will automatically be used to train Amazon‘s AI products.”

item.title: Statewide network launches to preserve South Carolina’s historic Black schools and legacy
item.description: ABC 4: “A new statewide network focused on preserving the history and legacy of South Carolina’s historic Black schools officially launched Thursday in Columbia. The South Carolina Historic Black Schools Preservation Network was launched by the Central Carolina Community Foundation in partnership with the University of South Carolina Center for Civil Rights History and Research.”

item.title: US Awards $125,000 to Preserve Ancient Nigerian Iron-Smelting Site
item.description: DNE Africa: “The United States has awarded a $125,000 grant to help preserve and digitally document an ancient iron-smelting site in Nigeria’s southeastern Enugu state, the U.S. Embassy in Nigeria said on Monday. The United States has awarded a $125,000 grant to help preserve and digitally document an ancient iron-smelting site in Nigeria’s southeastern Enugu state, the U.S. Embassy in Nigeria said on Monday. The grant, awarded through the Ambassadors Fund for Cultural Preservation (AFCP), will support the conservation and three-dimensional documentation of the Lejja archaeological site, as well as the recording of oral histories and traditional knowledge linked to its iron-working heritage.”

item.title: Tate Media Library
item.description: Distributed Denial of Secrets: “The files include individual clips, media from their AI Library, Editing Sandbox, Promos, Stock Video Archive, Video snippet files, and productions including Heroes of Wudan, Tales of Wudan, Immortal Dragon, Money Glitch, and Real Life Tate.” Not public; available to researchers and journalists only.

item.title: New Twitter launches, says Musk’s X gave up the name
item.description: Ars Technica: “Operation Bluebird, the Virginia-based startup trying to revive the allegedly abandoned ‘Twitter’ name and logo, announced Monday that it has launched its new social media network: Twitter.now.”

item.title: Bluesky adds an ‘algorithmic opt-out’ feature for those who don’t want to go viral
item.description: TechCrunch: “After adding support for longer videos just yesterday, open social network Bluesky on Thursday introduced a new algorithmic opt-out feature that allows users to stop their posts from appearing in the app’s main Discover feed. That algorithmic feed can currently surface any post on Bluesky’s network, as posts on the network are public by default.” Oh, like a Mastodon quiet post!

item.title: Tate brothers appear in court, asking to be released from jail during extradition fight
item.description: Associated Press: “Social media influencer Tristan Tate took the witness stand in federal court on Thursday and said he and his brother Andrew can’t adequately defend themselves from criminal sex charges if they have to remain in a Miami jail while fighting extradition to the United Kingdom.”

item.title: BBC chief proposes ‘public service algorithm’ with YouTube-style user-generated content
item.description: The Guardian: “The BBC director general has suggested opening up the BBC to YouTube-style user-generated content as he backed the idea of a ‘public service algorithm’ free from the interests of US tech companies.”

item.title: YouTubers can now include affiliate links to Amazon in their content
item.description: Engadget: “With this change, eligible YouTube creators will be able to link out to Amazon product listings from their videos. Videos, Shorts and livestreams on YouTube can all now tag items on Amazon, with the creator earning a commission on any purchases made from their links.”

item.title: US FTC probes YouTube over social media policies, Bloomberg News reports
item.description: Reuters: “The U.S. Federal Trade Commission has been investigating whether YouTube violated consumer protection laws by suspending users’ accounts ​and is in the final stages of preparing a ‌potential lawsuit, Bloomberg News reported on Thursday, citing people familiar with the matter.”

item.title: US servicemember, KPMG employee are targets of prediction markets crackdown
item.description: Wall Street Journal: This link goes to an MSN-syndicated version of the article which has no paywall. “Federal authorities are preparing charges against a U.S. servicemember suspected of placing Polymarket bets on military operations that earned him more than $1 million, part of a coming batch of insider trading cases, according to people familiar with the matter. The serviceman, who has been under scrutiny since the spring, made successful bets related to military strikes in Iran and Venezuela on the prediction market, the people said.”

item.title: Montgomery County teacher accused of targeting young girls on Snapchat
item.description: NBC Philadelphia: “Federal prosecutors have charged a Montgomery County elementary school teacher, alleging he used Snapchat to pose as a child and persuade young girls to create and send sexually explicit images and videos of themselves.”

item.title: No Easy Fix for Bogus Respondents in Online Opt-In Polls
item.description: Pew (PEW PEW PEW PEW PEW!): “… researchers have developed various ways to identify and purge bogus cases from survey samples. Approaches include 1) trap questions, sometimes called “attention checks,” that genuine respondents should always answer correctly, 2) automated prescreening services, and 3) matching respondents to a registered voter file. But how well do they work?” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Sainsbury’s staff eject wrong shopper after facial recognition alert – again
item.description: The Register: “UK supermarket giant Sainsbury’s temporarily suspended live facial recognition (LFR) at one of its stores after staff wrongly ejected a shopper in response to an alert – the second such incident this year.”

item.title: The One Big Issue That Connects the Data Center and Flock Backlash
item.description: Gizmodo: “The backlash to data centers seems to have reached its fever pitch this week when Liquid Death ran an advertisement with former NFL player and current podcaster Jason Kelce encouraging people to send their piss to data centers. You know you’ve lost the messaging war when a national brand and their celebrity endorser view pissing on you as a safe marketing bet.”

item.title: Another potential headache for US data centers — Trump tariffs
item.description: Politico: “The Trump administration is weighing a new round of sweeping tariffs on semiconductors, eight people familiar with discussions told POLITICO — despite warnings from tech companies that the move could doom U.S. hopes of dominating artificial intelligence.”

item.title: Google admits it will run the Tulsa data center
item.description: OK Energy Today: “Google confirmed this week it is the firm behind the massive data center campus being built near Owasso in Tulsa County. Project Clydesdale is a 506-acre campus in unincorporated Tulsa County and ground on the project was broken in October 2025 by Beale Infrastructure. But until this week, the end user had not been publicly identified. Now, Google says the campus will become part of its global data center network.”

item.title: The kids are generating images
item.description: Queens Chronicle: “Aliya Bonar, a mother in Glendale, says her 5-year-old son is already being told to use artificial intelligence in kindergarten classes. ‘He came back from one class and said that they were generating images,’ she told the Chronicle in an interview. That wasn’t what she expected from a public school coding class aimed at 5-year-olds.”

item.title: AI slopper in chief: Trump turns to social media amid tough questions
item.description: The Guardian: “Donald Trump knows the power of an image – of himself, with everyone from Vladimir Putin and Kim Jong-un to Kim Kardashian. How about George Washington? As the US president struggles to end his war with Iran, and with his approval ratings hitting the lowest levels of his second term, he has in recent weeks posted a series of AI-generated images of himself alongside key historical American figures.”

item.title: SK Telecom, Kakao and KT chosen for public AI service project
item.description: Korea JoongAng Daily: “The selected operators plan to introduce general-purpose AI chatbot services designed to outperform foreign AI models, AI agents that handle complex public administrative procedures on users’ behalf and specialized services developed in collaboration with startups.”

item.title: Mark Zuckerberg had a bold plan to replace Meta staff with AI. Here’s how it imploded.
item.description: Reuters: “To make its workforce ‘AI native,’ Meta explored slashing the size of many teams across the company by as much as 60% in two waves, internal documents show. Staff revolted – and hours before a big layoff in May, the CEO called off planning for further cuts.”

item.title: CoComelon production company to start using AI to produce mind-numbing content
item.description: AV Club: “CoComelon, the wibbly-wobbly YouTube phenomenon that turns toddlers into frothing monsters whenever it’s shut off and has made parents into unlikely media critics, is pivoting its content mill production toward AI, according to an in-depth report from tech vertical 404 Media.”

item.title: Business Titan Cops to Using AI to Pen Blockbuster WSJ Op-Ed Criticizing His Protégé Scott Bessent: ‘Of Course I Did’
item.description: Mediaite: “A billionaire investor who slammed U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent in an op-ed for The Wall Street Journal quickly copped to using artificial intelligence while writing the piece, according to a report. Stanley Druckenmiller, who once worked with Bessent and has been described as his ‘mentor,’ dismissed using AI, telling NOTUS it was the equivalent of using a calculator to solve a math problem.”

item.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda
item.description: The Guardian: “A pro-Israel messaging website badged with the name of a thinktank that does not exist has published more than half a million words in nine days, built on a commercial platform that promises to optimize content so that AI chatbots will cite it.”

item.title: Need spiritual guidance? Gurus join chatbot trend as people turn to AI for answers
item.description: Associated Press: “This unfettered access — which can be challenging to find among human gurus — is what’s drawing more people to AI for spiritual guidance. This is a big step, particularly in Hinduism, where gurus are part of culture and deemed necessary to attain moksha — liberation from the cycle of birth, death and reincarnation. The word guru in Sanskrit means ‘dispeller of darkness.'”

item.title: Judge blocks Pentagon blacklist of Anthropic as supply chain risk
item.description: CNBC: “A San Francisco federal judge on Thursday ruled that the Pentagon’s blacklisting of artificial intelligence giant Anthropic earlier this year was illegal.”

item.title: The Scandinavian Solution to A.I. in Schools
item.description: New York Times: “The economists David Strömberg, Victor Lei and Yanhui Wu found that while A.I. use raised homework scores among students, it lowered “monthly exam scores by 20 percent within six months. High-stakes entrance-exam scores fall by 18 and 24 percent,” with student performance worsening over time. The students with the greatest negative effects on their exam scores appeared to be rushing through their homework by outsourcing to A.I.”

item.title: New hurricane recovery technology being tested on Florida roads during peak season
item.description: University of South Florida: “Working with transportation professionals across Florida, including those at the Florida Department of Transportation and Sarasota County, [Professor Hao] Zhou is developing AI tools to help transportation officials assess storm damage more efficiently, improve traffic signal restoration and better understand transportation needs after hurricanes. The first technology, an AI-powered dashcam, is expected to begin testing later this fall.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Institute for Justice Unveils New Database Tracking Cancelations of License Plate Reader Contracts
item.description: Institute for Justice: “As backlash grows against the warrantless use of automated license plate reader (ALPR) cameras throughout the country, local governments are increasingly deciding to end their use of these cameras. Today, the Institute for Justice (IJ) unveiled a new database tracking local governments that have canceled or not renewed contracts with ALPR providers since the beginning of 2025.”

item.title: Digital newspaper archive: free access to collections of newspapers and periodicals of provincial or local circulation
item.description: National Library of Argentina, and machine-translated from Spanish: “Continuing the review and analysis process regarding access to digital collections, initiated months ago, the Mariano Moreno National Library has decided to provide free access to the issues of some local and provincial newspapers and periodicals. Unlike major national media outlets, these periodicals constitute a detailed record of the history, experiences, and identity of the diverse regions and communities of our country, representing a fundamental resource for researchers and citizens seeking to reconstruct the past.”

item.title: Ocean Views: New Tools to Assess Ocean Monitoring Efforts Off of California’s Coast
item.description: California Cooperative Oceanic Fisheries Investigations: “Southern California Current waters have the reputation of being among the most well monitored stretch of ocean on earth. But just how well do we monitor the Southern California Current Ecosystem? Until recently, no one created a comprehensive inventory of ocean monitoring programs off of California. However, a group of ten talented, recently graduated UCLA Environmental Science seniors worked with CalCOFI to create this inventory with a robust metadata attribute table and produce an extraordinary interactive GIS map of monitoring programs within 13.4 miles from the coast, including state waters (3 nautical miles offshore) plus an additional ten miles.”

item.title: Bubbles.town: Four Months Later
item.description: Brennan.Day: “It was near the end of April when I interviewed the creator of Bubbles.town, Benjamin Behnke, and I feel as though I’ve been using the platform for enough time to give a more long-term review of it now. Here are some of my thoughts, and if you disagree with any please drop a comment!”

item.title: Vanderbilt Television News Archive launches new web platform with improved search capabilities
item.description: Vanderbilt University: “The Jean and Alexander Heard Libraries have launched a new web platform and improved database for the Vanderbilt Television News Archive, one of the most extensive and complete archives of television news in the world. The new system includes enhancements to the archive’s search capabilities, the option to browse by date, automatic delivery of loaned materials, single sign-on for Vanderbilt and sponsoring institutions, and more.”

item.title: Bluesky now lets you upload 10-minute long videos
item.description: TechCrunch: “Social network Bluesky said on Tuesday that it is now increasing video limits on the platform to 10 minutes. Previously, the platform allowed three-minute videos, a limit that it raised last year. This makes it more competitive with other text-based platforms that by default allow for shorter video uploads.”

item.title: 1000s of affordable housing subsidies will end in the next 5 years. A new database will help Pa. get in front of the issue.
item.description: Spotlight PA: “In an effort to better monitor the supply of affordable housing, Pennsylvania will create a searchable database of properties that are required to offer discounted rents and track when those requirements expire. The database, which was included in the state budget deal that lawmakers passed in July, is intended to bring more transparency to an issue that could affect thousands of Pennsylvanians who live in properties that are subsidized by state and federal programs.”

item.title: YouTube Uses Set-Piece Speech To Protest That It’s Not A “Villain” Intent On Toppling TV
item.description: Deadline: “YouTube has a message for the television industry: We are a friend, not a foe. In a set-piece speech at the Edinburgh TV Festival on Wednesday, Pedro Pina, YouTube’s vice president in EMEA, said the video-sharing platform is not a ‘villain’ for the traditional broadcasting business.”

item.title: Car thefts, garda chases and fake licences: Irish accounts showing illegality persist on TikTok
item.description: The Journal (Ireland): “DOZENS OF TIKTOK accounts showing car thefts and dangerous driving remain online, a week and a half after five teenagers died and four family members in another car were injured in the M9 crash. There is also evidence the social media platform’s algorithm is presenting such videos to users who have previously viewed them – essentially boosting their visibility.”

item.title: A national peatland database for the Republic of Ireland
item.description: Data In Brief: “This article presents a national peatland database for the Republic of Ireland, covering not only undrained, near-intact bogs with absent land use and management at present but also peatlands that have been reclaimed for grassland, forestry and peat extraction (industrial and domestic) land uses.”

item.title: A nosy polar bear and a lucky squirrel: Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 shortlist
item.description: BBC: “The overall winners will be announced on Tuesday 13 October 2026, followed by an exhibition at the Natural History Museum in London from Friday 16 October 2026. Scroll down to explore other highly commended works from the competition.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Announcing Guildhall 3D with Cradle of English
item.description: Spatial Heritage Review: “Guildhall 3D is the most complete digital 3D record of the interior of the Great Hall at the City of London Corporation’s Guildhall in London, a prime example of layered historical architecture literally festooned with heraldry, statuary, and meaning.”

item.title: Coconut Grove Playhouse’s 521 shows now in free digital archive
item.description: Biscayne Bay Beacon: “Every program and every star from the Coconut Grove Playhouse’s 50-year run is now searchable online, thanks to a digital archive that went live the week of Aug. 17. Arnold Mittelman, the playhouse’s last and longest-serving artistic director, who led the theater for 21 years, spent two and a half years assembling the collection… with a Knight Foundation grant of more than $100,000.”

item.title: Meta’s social media settlement leaves its money machine unscathed
item.description: Reuters: “Roughly a month ago, Instagram head Adam ​Mosseri had a meeting with representatives of the attorneys generals in which he said Meta would appeal any adverse verdict, as it is already doing following a billion-dollar child safety ​ruling won by New Mexico, according to people familiar with the matter. But Mosseri said Meta was ready to make constructive changes to its platform, assuming it could work out a deal, the sources added, requesting anonymity as the meeting was private.”

item.title: OnlyFans Millionaires: Site Says 5,076 Creators Have Earned More Than $1 Million to Date
item.description: Variety: “Since the 2016 launch of OnlyFans, which is known for its porn-friendly policies, 5,076 creators have made over $1 million on the platform, the company said Tuesday. In total, OnlyFans — which takes a 20% cut of gross revenue generated by the site — said it has paid out more than $30 billion to creators in the last 10 years, including $6.3 billion for the year ended Nov. 30, 2025.”

item.title: Confirmed: Google Search Rolling Out google.com/goto Tracking Parameters
item.description: Search Engine Roundtable: “Google Search seems like it is rolling out the google.com/goto URL as a passthrough URL within the search results that it began testing in July 2026. This seems like a way for Google to help prevent scraping of its search results by third-party tools and AI companies, but Google has not yet commented on this goto URL parameter.”

item.title: P.E.I. teenager goes viral with ‘Manne of Green Gables’ videos
item.description: Canadian Press: “Towards the back of [Shop and Play], behind rows of P.E.I.-themed merchandise and postcards of Confederation Bridge, visitors can pay to dress up and take photos as the province’s main fictional export, Anne of Green Gables. On May 24, the shop posted a video of [Jack] Pickering giving a walkthrough of the parlour wearing an Anne costume consisting of a green dress, straw hat and a wig of her infamous red hair and braids.”

item.title: Poland asks EU to fine Meta €250m over scam Facebook ads
item.description: Notes from Poland: “Poland has formally requested that the European Commission fine Meta, the owner of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, €250 million (1.1 billion zloty) for failing to tackle fraudulent advertising on its platforms. Its decision follows a high-profile campaign by Rafał Brzoska, the billionaire owner of Polish delivery giant InPost, over scam adverts on Facebook that exploit fake images of him and other prominent Polish public figures, including President Karol Nawrocki.”

item.title: Pro-Russian hackers claim responsibility for major cyberattack on Norway’s public digital services
item.description: Associated Press: “A pro-Russian hacker group on Wednesday claimed responsibility for a cyberattack that has affected multiple Norwegian government digital services over the past three days. The cyberattack has been ongoing since Monday, said Are Kvistad, a spokesperson for the Norwegian Digitalization Agency (Digdir), the state body in charge of making Norway’s public services more digital and user-friendly, told The Associated Press.”

item.title: Meta, TikTok, YouTube and LinkedIn didn’t act on 77% of misinformation reported during Áras race
item.description: The Journal (Ireland): “SOCIAL MEDIA COMPANIES failed to act on the vast majority of electoral disinformation reported by researchers ahead of last year’s presidential election, a new report shows. The report also criticised the companies for not demonstrating an understanding of the context around the election, which was held in October last year.”

item.title: Brazil: Amnesty International experiment exposes Meta’s failure to catch election-related disinformation ads on Facebook
item.description: Amnesty International, and I will swear to you on the religious volume of your choice that I did not deliberately put these articles together: “To investigate how Facebook handled election-related disinformation in advertising, Amnesty International conducted an experiment by submitting ‘mock’ ads containing election-related disinformation to Facebook. The content ranged from ads alleging election fraud to ads that used disinformation to advocate for a military takeover. The experiment found that eight of the submitted ads were accepted, while the remaining seven were flagged for identity verification as they appeared to be related to a social issue, election or politics, rather than being rejected specifically because they contained election-related disinformation.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: 31 Medieval Manuscripts from the Czech National Library Now Available Online
item.description: Medievalists.net: “Thirty-one medieval manuscripts from the National Library of the Czech Republic are now available online, offering a new look at medieval medicine, religion, law and science. Among them is a medical manuscript containing a previously unknown copy of advice written for Holy Roman Emperor Sigismund.”

item.title: Community rallies to stop closure of National Archives facility
item.description: AsAm News: “Dozens of sign carrying community members gathered in front of the National Archives and Records Administration offices near San Francisco today to urge NARA to keep the facility open.”

item.title: Anna’s Archive Owes $340 Million, Lost Several Domains, but It’s Still Online
item.description: TorrentFreak: “When Anna’s Archive suffered widespread downtime earlier this month, many users feared a legal crackdown. Instead, the site was reportedly targeted by a coordinated assault on its network infrastructure. Just as it did after facing $340 million in damages and losing several domains earlier this year, the Archive quickly bounced back.”

item.title: Andrew Tate exaggerates and did not own supercars in photos, his lawyers say
item.description: BBC: “Controversial influencer Andrew Tate portrays himself as ‘uberwealthy’ but did not own cars and a yacht featured on his social media and exaggerated his lifestyle for online attention, his legal representatives have said. Tate and his brother Tristan are currently being held in a Florida jail but are seeking release on bail while they await the outcome of extradition proceedings.”

item.title: Dollywood Site Temporarily Crashes After Fans Rush to Honor Dolly Parton
item.description: Parade: “Within an hour of the public announcement, an overwhelming surge of visitors rushed to Dollywood.com to check operational updates, review travel plans, and secure park tickets. The sudden spike in web traffic briefly overwhelmed the Pigeon Forge, Tennessee, destination’s servers, The New York Post reported, temporarily replacing the standard homepage with an error screen citing abnormally high volume.” Posterity, I have never seen such Internet-wide mourning.

item.title: Explore a rare collection of LGBTQ+ children’s books dating back to 1969.
item.description: Literary Hub: “The Mechanics’ Institute, one of the oldest cultural institutions on the West Coast, is now home to a thrilling archive of LGBTQ+ children’s literature. The Tarpey–Schwed LGBT Families Children’s Book Special Collection features more than 200 queer-friendly kids’ books published between 1969 and 2023. Titles like Heather Has Two Mommies and Lucy Goes to the Country show the evolution of queer representation in children’s literature over five decades, offering a rare opportunity for families and researchers alike.”

item.title: How High School Media Programs Prepare Future Creators
item.description: Ed Circuit: “From newspapers and radio stations to podcasts, livestreams, AI, and digital storytelling, today’s high school media programs are preparing students for careers that didn’t exist just a decade ago.”

item.title: California’s crackdown on addictive social media feeds for kids will proceed as platforms appeal
item.description: Courthouse News: “TikTok, Meta and YouTube must comply with California’s crackdown on addictive algorithmic feeds for kids while their appeals play out, a federal judge ruled, rejecting the platforms’ bid to keep the law from being enforced while they seek review in the Ninth Circuit.”

item.title: California lawmakers vote to increase transparency over influencers’ paid political posts
item.description: Spectrum News: ” The California Senate passed a bill Monday that would fine content creators who don’t disclose they were paid to post in support of a political candidate or issue on the ballot. California, along with Texas, already requires content creators to include payment disclaimers on their political posts. The goal of this year’s bill is to better enforce the law.”

item.title: The Search Engine Privacy Index: What Every Search Engine Really Knows About You
item.description: Private Internet Access: “Interest in privacy-focused engines has particularly grown in recent years. After Google’s AI-heavy search changes in May 2026, DuckDuckGo reported a sharp rise in app installs across the U.S., peaking at 30.5% daily growth. That shift led us at Private Internet Access to review the privacy policies and public documentation of 24 search engines, comparing how they collect, retain, and share user data.”

item.title: UGA project receives $743,658 grant to preserve colonial history
item.description: University of Georgia: “The three-year project, Many Eyes on the Road to Revolution in Colonial Georgia, will examine the state’s history from 1732 to 1798…. The project will digitize more than 12,000 pages of historical documents and make them freely available through the Digital Library of Georgia. Researchers also will preserve archaeological collections and develop educational resources for students and the public.” Good morning, Internet…
